question.explanation:
If we denote

\[ P(t): t<1, \]

our statement can be written as

\[ \forall t \in \mathbb{Q}, \, P(t). \]

Negating this, we obtain

\[ \neg \left( \forall t \in \mathbb{Q}, \, P(t) \right) \equiv \exists t \in \mathbb{Q}, \, \neg P(t). \]

Finally, $\exists t \in \mathbb{Q}, \, \neg P(t)$ reads as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $t \in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $t \geq 1.$

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ Some composite numbers are not divisible by $3.$
question.choice1: All composite numbers are divisible by $3.$
question.choice2: All composite numbers are not divisible by $3.$
question.choice3: Some composite numbers are not divisible by $3.$
question.choice4: Some composite numbers are divisible by $3.$
question.explanation:
Let $C$ be the set of all composite numbers. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $x \in C$ such that $x$ is not divisible by $3.$

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\exists x \in C, \, x \textrm{ is not divisible by $3$}.$

Negating this, we obtain \begin{align*} \neg \left( \exists x \in C, \, x \textrm{ is not divisible by $3$} \right) &\equiv \forall x \in C, \, \neg \big( x \textrm{ is not divisible by $3$} \big) \\[3pt] &\equiv \forall x \in C, \, x \textrm{ is divisible by $3$} \end{align*}

which reads

$\qquad$ For all $x \in C,$ $x \textrm{ is divisible by $3$}.$

or simply

$\qquad$ All composite numbers are divisible by $3.$

To negate the universal statement $\forall a \in \overline{V}, \, \neg H(a),$ we flip the quantifier to existential and negate the predicate:

\begin{align*} \neg \left( \forall a \in \overline{V}, \, \neg H(a) \right) &\equiv \exists a \in \overline{V}, \,\neg\neg H(a) \\[5pt] &\equiv \exists a \in \bbox[2pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\overline{V}}, \, \bbox[2pt, Gainsboro]{\color{blue} H(a)} \end{align*}

example.title: Identifying the Formula For Negating a Quantified Statement

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ Every universal statement is not true.
question.choice2: Some universal statements are not true.
question.choice4: All universal statements are not true.
question.explanation:
Let $U$ be the set of all universal statements. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ For all $x \in U,$ $x$ is not true.

Introducing the universal quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\forall x \in U, \, \textrm{$x$ is not true}.$

Negating this, we obtain \begin{align*} \neg \left( \forall x \in U, \, \textrm{$x$ is not true} \right) &\equiv \exists x \in U, \, \neg \big( \textrm{$x$ is not true} \big) \\[5pt] &\equiv \exists x \in U, \, \textrm{$x$ is true} \end{align*}

which reads

$\qquad$ There exists $x \in U$ such that $x$ is true.

or simply

$\qquad$ Some universal statements are true.

question.text:
Negate the following statement:

$\qquad$ At least one sequence is geometric.
question.choice3: At least one sequence is not geometric.
question.choice4: At least one sequence is geometric.
question.explanation:
Let $S$ be the set of all sequences. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $s \in S$ such that $s$ is geometric.

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\exists s \in S, \, \textrm{$s$ is geometric}.$

Negating this, we obtain \begin{align*} \neg \left( \exists s \in S, \, \textrm{$s$ is geometric} \right) &\equiv \forall s \in S, \, \neg \big( \textrm{$s$ is geometric} \big) \\[3pt] &\equiv \forall s \in S, \, \textrm{$s$ is not geometric} \end{align*}

which reads

$\qquad$ For all $s \in S,$ $s$ is not geometric.

or simply

$\qquad$ Every sequence is not geometric.
